planting.note: Mount or pot in a small amount of coarse, fast-draining bark mix and disturb the roots as little as possible; Phalaenopsis amboinensis resents repotting and may sulk for a year or more afterward.

directions: Phalaenopsis amboinensis is a warm-growing monopodial epiphyte from the Moluccas, Sulawesi, and New Guinea, with thick dark-green leaves and an arching, often branching inflorescence of waxy, star-shaped flowers in yellow to greenish-yellow heavily barred with cinnamon-brown or maroon transverse stripes. Unlike many of its relatives, a single flower spike can continue producing new flowers intermittently for months or even years, so growers should never cut back a spent-looking spike while it remains green. This species has been an important parent behind many spotted and barred yellow Phalaenopsis hybrids grown commercially today. Keep in bright, filtered light year-round with consistent warmth, high humidity, and a coarse, quick-draining mount or bark mix that never stays soggy.
sources: American Orchid Society — Phalaenopsis species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Phalaenopsis amboinensis

planting.note: Grow mounted or in a slatted basket with open bark mix so roots dry quickly after watering; Phalaenopsis sumatrana is prone to crown and root rot if water sits in the leaf axils or media overnight.

directions: Phalaenopsis sumatrana is native to the lowland and lower-montane forests of Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, and Borneo, where it grows as an epiphyte on tree trunks in dappled, filtered light. Its waxy, long-lasting flowers are pale greenish-yellow to cream, overlaid with bold reddish-brown to maroon longitudinal stripes, and are carried on an arching spike that can rebloom repeatedly from the same growth point over successive seasons. Many clones release a distinct fragrance at night, a trait thought to attract moth pollinators in its native habitat. Provide bright indirect light, steady warmth, and high humidity, allowing the coarse bark medium to approach dryness between thorough waterings.
sources: American Orchid Society — Phalaenopsis species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Phalaenopsis sumatrana

planting.note: Pot in a small clay or slatted container with coarse bark mix; Phalaenopsis tetraspis prefers to be slightly pot-bound and only needs repotting every two to three years.

directions: Phalaenopsis tetraspis is native to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and nearby parts of western Sumatra, and takes its name from its unusual four separate pollinia, a trait that distinguishes it from the two fused pollinia pairs found in most other Phalaenopsis species. Broad, flat, waxy white flowers are variably overlaid with pink to magenta spotting that ranges from nearly clear 'alba' forms to heavily speckled clones, and individual flowers can remain open and fresh for two months or longer. Flower spikes often branch and can continue flowering intermittently for an extended period, making this a popular species among collectors seeking long-lived blooms. Grow in bright, filtered light with warm, humid, buoyant air and a fast-draining bark or sphagnum mix.
sources: American Orchid Society — Phalaenopsis species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Phalaenopsis tetraspis

planting.note: Mount on bark or pot loosely in coarse orchid bark; Phalaenopsis speciosa is a compact grower and does best slightly pot-bound with roots exposed to moving air.

directions: Phalaenopsis speciosa is a compact, fragrant species endemic to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, bearing twisted, slightly recurved sepals and petals in colors that vary widely between individual plants, from pale cream and yellow to deep maroon-purple, often with contrasting striping near the base. Several flowers open in succession on a modestly arching spike, and the fragrance is most noticeable during the warmer part of the day. As a smaller-growing species it suits windowsill culture better than many of its larger relatives. Provide bright, indirect light, consistent warmth and humidity, and a free-draining bark mix that dries somewhat between waterings.
sources: American Orchid Society — Phalaenopsis species culture sheet

common_name: King Orchid (Sydney Rock Lily, Rock Orchid)

planting.note: Mount on a slab, in a basket, or pot in a very open bark-and-rock mix; Dendrobium speciosum grows naturally on exposed cliff faces and tree forks and dislikes a constantly moist root zone.

directions: Dendrobium speciosum, the King Orchid or Sydney Rock Lily, is a large lithophytic and epiphytic species native to the cliffs, rock outcrops, and tree trunks of eastern Australia from Queensland to Victoria, and is one of the floral emblems associated with New South Wales. Thick, stout canes topped with a few leathery leaves produce long, arching racemes that can carry well over a hundred small, fragrant, cream to pale yellow flowers in a dramatic spring display. Mature specimens need very bright light approaching that of full sun in cultivation, along with a distinctly cooler, drier winter rest to encourage the following season's flowering. Mount on a slab or grow in a chunky, well-aerated mix, and expect this species to take several years to reach flowering size from a young division.
sources: American Orchid Society — Dendrobium species culture sheet
Australian National Botanic Gardens — Dendrobium speciosum profile
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Dendrobium speciosum

planting.note: Grow in a small pot or basket with open bark mix and give a distinct cooler, drier rest after the canes mature in fall; Dendrobium secundum is deciduous and sets flower buds along bare canes during this rest period.

directions: Dendrobium secundum, widely called the Toothbrush Orchid, is native to Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, where it grows as a warm-climate epiphyte on trees in seasonally dry forest. Its common name comes from the dense, one-sided cluster of small, fragrant pink to magenta flowers that all face the same direction along the upper part of the cane, each flower showing a contrasting bright orange lip. The slender canes are deciduous or semi-deciduous, dropping their leaves before flowering in response to a dry season, so cultivated plants bloom best after a cooler, drier rest period in late winter. Grow in bright light with a free-draining mix, watering heavily through the warm growing season and tapering off sharply once new growth matures.
sources: American Orchid Society — Dendrobium species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Dendrobium secundum

common_name: Cuthbertson's Dendrobium (New Guinea Alpine Miniature Orchid)

planting.note: Pot small divisions in fine-grade sphagnum moss rather than bark; Dendrobium cuthbertsonii has a tiny, fibrous root system that dries out quickly in coarse media and needs constant, cool moisture.

directions: Dendrobium cuthbertsonii is a tiny alpine epiphyte restricted to the high-altitude cloud forests of New Guinea, where cool, misty, buoyant conditions persist year-round regardless of season. Despite a mature plant reaching only an inch or two tall, it produces disproportionately large, long-lasting flowers — often remaining open for two to six months — in an exceptionally wide range of colors including red, orange, pink, purple, and white, frequently with bicolor patterning. Unlike most warm-growing Dendrobium species, this one requires consistently cool temperatures year-round, constant moisture at the roots, and very high humidity, making it a specialist's plant best suited to a terrarium, cloud forest case, or cool greenhouse rather than a typical warm windowsill. Keep evenly moist in fine sphagnum with bright, filtered light and steady air movement.
sources: American Orchid Society — Dendrobium species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Dendrobium cuthbertsonii

planting.note: Grow in a pot with coarse bark mix sized to the root mass; Cattleya amethystoglossa forms tall, heavy canes and benefits from a sturdy container or stake to keep top-heavy growths upright.

directions: Cattleya amethystoglossa is a tall bifoliate species from the Bahia region of Brazil, with slender canes reaching several feet in height and paired leathery leaves at the top of each mature growth. Multiple sprays of fragrant, heavily spotted rose-pink flowers open from the newest growths, each bloom showing a prominent amethyst-purple blotch on the lip that gives the species its name. It is among the most floriferous of the bifoliate Cattleyas, with well-grown specimens carrying dozens of flowers across several spikes at once. Provide strong, bright light, good air movement, and a pronounced drop in watering frequency after flowering to let the canes harden before the next growth cycle begins.
sources: American Orchid Society — Cattleya species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Cattleya amethystoglossa

planting.note: Pot in a well-draining bark mix sized just slightly larger than the root mass; Cattleya loddigesii flowers best when kept somewhat pot-bound and is not disturbed every year.

directions: Cattleya loddigesii is a bifoliate species native to Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, named for the Loddiges nursery of London that introduced many South American orchids to European cultivation in the nineteenth century. Slender, cylindrical canes carry two leathery leaves and produce autumn sprays of pale lavender-pink, lightly fragrant flowers with a frilled, deeper-colored lip. The species has long been valued by breeders for passing on pastel coloring, a compact, floriferous habit, and good autumn bloom timing to countless modern Cattleya-alliance hybrids. Grow in bright light with good airflow, watering well during active growth and allowing a modest dry rest once the canes mature in fall.
sources: American Orchid Society — Cattleya species culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online: Cattleya loddigesii

planting.note: Mount on a small slab or pot shallowly in a fine bark mix; Cattleya nobilior has a creeping rhizome and compact roots that resent being buried deeply.

directions: Cattleya nobilior is a compact, creeping species from the seasonally flooded grasslands and gallery forests of central Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay, growing low to its support with short, stout pseudobulbs. Flowers open singly or in small clusters close to the newest growth, typically in shades of rose-purple with a darker, ruffled lip, and are large relative to the small size of the plant. Along with the closely related Cattleya walkeriana, this species has been widely used by breeders to produce compact, early-flowering miniature Cattleya hybrids suited to small growing spaces. Provide strong light, a distinct dry rest after flowering, and a shallow mount or pot that allows the rhizome to creep without being buried.
sources: American Orchid Society — Cattleya species culture sheet
